Where deeds are recorded

Milwaukee County deeds and mortgages are filed with the Register of Deeds, Room 103 at 901 N. 9th Street, Milwaukee, WI 53233. You can drop papers off or mail them. The counter runs 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays; call (414) 278-4021.

Deeds are one task among several. Staff also scan and index corporation papers and military discharges, log informal probate instruments, hold financing statements, collect the transfer fee and issue birth, death and marriage certificates.

Roughly 924,216 people lived here as of July 1, 2025, every one inside a city or village, because no unincorporated towns exist in this county. A single office serves all 19 municipalities, 10 cities and 9 villages.

Recording costs

Filing an ordinary document is $30 however many pages it runs. Plats, certified copies and the sale transfer fee are billed on top. The counter takes cash, checks and money orders payable to the Register of Deeds, and no credit or debit cards.

Document or serviceCost
Standard document (not a plat)$30
Certified copy bought at recording$2 first page, $1 each added page, $1 to certify
Subdivision plat$50
Condominium plat$100 review (separate check) plus $50 recording
Department of Transportation plat$25
Termination of decedent's interest$30

Anything else sent in with a plat is charged the standard $30 apiece. For a sale, the receipt for your transfer return shows the fee, which you settle at the counter together with recording.

How the transfer fee is figured

Here is the math. A non-exempt conveyance owes 30 cents on each $100 of value, with any leftover fraction treated as a whole $100. Put another way, $3 per $1,000. Wis. Stat. 77.22 assigns it to the seller (the grantor), and staff take payment at the moment the deed arrives.

Value is whatever was paid or will be paid, liens included. A gift, a token-price deed or a swap is measured instead by the likely open market price between a willing buyer and a willing seller (s. 77.21). The county retains 20 percent of its collections and forwards the balance to the state (s. 77.24).

Section 77.25 carves out exemptions. People selling or inheriting a house see these the most:

  • Property passing by will, descent or survivorship.
  • A lender or land contract vendor taking title through foreclosure or a deed in lieu.
  • Tax and assessment sale deeds.
  • Gifts within the family, like parent to child, stepparent to stepchild or grandparent to grandchild, given for little or nothing.
  • Property of $1,000 or less in value.
  • Paperwork whose only purpose is to secure or release a debt.

Staff won't rule on whether your exemption holds, so describe it correctly on the return. Local governments may not layer their own charge on a conveyance the state fee exempts (s. 77.256).

What to bring or mail

Pack three things: the signed original deed, the transfer return receipt and your payment. Section 77.22(2) requires the return with every conveyance, and without it the register refuses the deed. The Department of Revenue hosts the return in My Tax Account, and no username or password is needed to file.

  • The original deed, finished before it is handed in.
  • The return receipt, or the exemption reason printed on it.
  • Cash or a check to the Register of Deeds covering $30 and whatever transfer fee applies.
  • Your name and address as the return recipient, because the original is posted back to you.

Wis. Stat. 706.05 sets the content rules. The deed needs the signatures the law demands and enough description of land and parties for the office to index it. Papers indexed in the real estate records, mortgage or land contract modifications and subordination agreements all need the full legal description, and a modification adds the original's document number.

Staff don't draft papers, keep blank deed forms or opine on legal soundness. You can write your own or use an attorney or title company. For return questions, contact the Department of Revenue at (608) 266-1594 or eRETR@revenue.wi.gov.

How long recording takes

Allow three to five business days for recording, handled in arrival order, and one to two weeks for the original to come back by post. Because nothing is recorded instantly, leave slack before a closing date. To check on a pending document, email RODrecordings@milwaukeecountywi.gov or call (414) 278-4005.

If a cash buyer wants a quick close, ask the closing agent when the deed gets to the Register of Deeds and whether any return exemption fits your transfer.

Removing a deceased owner from the deed

Record a termination of decedent's interest. Where a deed lists both spouses, you file form HT-110, a transfer return claiming s. 77.25(11) for passage by will, descent or survivorship, a copy of the deed already of record, and $30. The county has dropped its old requirement for a tax bill copy or death certificate.

A recorded transfer on death document works the same way, only with form TOD-110 and the s. 77.25(11m) exemption. Forms and instructions are posted by the Wisconsin Register of Deeds Association. If you're selling an inherited house, check with the title company on whether this filing must precede closing.

Changing ownership any other way, for example adding or dropping a name, means a fresh deed with its own return. The office can't write it.

This free online service emails you when your exact name shows up as grantor or grantee on a recorded document. It can't stop fraud, but it gives early warning if a deed or mortgage appears that you never signed. It suits owners of rentals, vacant homes and inherited houses waiting for sale.

Selling in a split owner and renter county

The county is almost evenly split between owners and renters. The owner-occupied rate is 49.9 percent, the median owner-occupied home is valued at $230,700 and median gross rent is $1,101. The county has 392,399 households and 429,425 housing units. These are county-wide numbers; your own city or village treasurer can supply the actual tax bill before you price the house.

Free legal help with deeds

Staff can't advise you legally, but the county points to two resources. The Marquette Volunteer Legal Clinic offers free, confidential, brief advice at House of Peace Community Center, 1702 W. Walnut Street, on Tuesdays from 4 to 6 p.m., with sign-in from 3:30 p.m. Its number is (414) 933-1300. The Lawyer Referral and Information Service takes calls Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Frequently asked questions

What is the recording charge?

$30 a document, any page count, with a transfer fee added on most sales. Plats cost $25 to $50, and condominium plats need a separate $100 review check. Pay by cash, check or money order.

What transfer fee does a seller pay?

Thirty cents per $100 of value, the same as $3 per $1,000, set by Wis. Stat. 77.22. It's taken from the seller as the deed is filed. Exempt transfers, like those by will or foreclosure, pay nothing.

Is the transfer return optional?

No. Every conveyance needs one, and the office treats the receipt as mandatory. An exempt transfer still files a return that states the exemption.

When does the original come back?

It's mailed to the return name and address on the document, one to two weeks after the three to five days of recording. Need proof sooner? Buy a certified copy when you record.

Can this office help with tax bills?

No, it only records documents and collects the transfer fee. Contact the treasurer of the city or village where the house is for balances and payoffs.

Office location and hours

Find the office inside the Northern Building, Room 260, 305 E. Walnut Street, Green Bay. Letters go to P.O. Box 23600, Green Bay, WI 54305-3600, and calls to 920-448-4470.

The doors are open Monday to Thursday from 7:30 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., and Friday mornings from 7:30 to 11:30. Real estate documents brought in by hand must arrive sooner: by 4:30 p.m. on Monday to Thursday, or by 10:30 a.m. Friday. Plan any Friday or late-afternoon closing around the earlier time, and phone the office first.

Every deed, land contract, mortgage and plat in the county ends up in this one office, which also handles vital records. Staff stamp each filing with its date and exact time (s. 59.43) and keep them in arrival order. Your house can be in any municipality; the deed still comes here.

Tag-less recording and the Swift Agreement

Brown County records without a paper tag. Anyone who sends paper documents for recording must include a completed Swift Agreement, which sets up access to the official copy once the document is recorded.

Once the deed is on record, an email arrives with a secure link. It lets you print three copies and lapses after seven days. Save the PDF the day it shows up if you want a permanent copy for the closing binder.

State law adds a delivery rule. A register must send recorded documents to the recipient the submitter names once adequate postage is provided, unless the submitter agrees to another arrangement (s. 59.43(1c)(g)). Put the recipient and an email address on the Swift Agreement so the link reaches the right person.

Searching land records

The county's land records search system is called Laredo, and it is available by advance appointment only. Call 920-448-4470 to book a time. Do not count on a same-day walk-in search the morning of a closing.

Copy prices are set by the state (s. 59.43(2)(b)): $2 for page one, $1 for every page after it, and $1 more if you want the copy certified. A seller rarely has to search personally. The title company runs the search that supports the sale, and all it needs from you is the parcel number printed on your tax bill.

Recording fees

The flat charge for a deed, mortgage or similar document is $30 (s. 59.43(2)(ag)), payable up front.

Document or serviceFee
Deed, mortgage, satisfaction or land contract$30
Cemetery, subdivision or condominium plat$50
Copy of a recorded document$2 first page, $1 each added page
Certification of a copy$1 more
State transfer fee (if the sale is not exempt)Paid by the seller, on top of the recording fee

Both charges are due when the deed is accepted, so settle them in one visit or one e-recording batch.

Transfer fee on a home sale

Under s. 77.22 the seller owes $3 per $1,000 of value, which works out to 30 cents for each $100 or part of $100. The base is the sale price, and a mortgage the buyer assumes counts toward it. When a property is given away with no price, report the full value estimated on the newest tax bill. Furniture, appliances and other personal property belong on their own line, outside the fee base.

Local wrinkles to know:

  • Howard and Wrightstown spill partly into Outagamie County. If your parcels straddle two counties, file one return per county.
  • Finishing a land contract with a deed triggers no second charge when the contract itself was recorded with the proper fee (s. 77.25(17)).
  • Local governments cannot add their own fee to a transfer the state exempts (s. 77.256).
  • List each grantor and each grantee separately on the return.

Behind the scenes, the register hands the month's fees and returns to the county treasurer by the 15th, and the county retains 20 percent (ss. 77.23 and 77.24). Exemptions are listed in s. 77.25 and include transfers by will, parent-to-child gifts and foreclosure deeds.

Why deeds get rejected

Two things sink a deed at the counter: a missed format rule in s. 59.43(2m), or a Social Security number on the page. One failing document can hold up a whole related set. Run down this list before signing:

  • Leave the top right corner of page one empty, a square of 3 by 3 inches.
  • List the parcel identification number of every parcel the deed covers.
  • Put a return address on page one, unless you record electronically.
  • Use plain white paper of 20 pound weight or heavier, 8.5 inches wide and either 11 or 14 inches long. Hinged pages are out.
  • Write in black, blue or red ink, and print the grantor, grantee and notary names so they can be read.
  • Strip out every Social Security number.

Staff do not check the stated value or an exemption claim, so accuracy rests with whoever files. Deliberately misstating value on a transfer return is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, a year in county jail, or both.

Before closing day

A deed that bounces at the counter can push a closing back a day or more, so it pays to prepare early. Here is a short list of what to settle in the week before.

  • Confirm who is sending the deed: the title company, an attorney or you. If it is you, decide whether it goes by mail, by hand or electronically.
  • Ask whoever drafted the deed to confirm the format rules were followed, since a rejected deed means redoing the signatures.
  • Decide whether any exemption applies. If one does, the return still shows the value and names the exemption.
  • Check which municipality your house is in, then see who collects the tax bill. Recording and tax payment are two separate counters.
  • Write down the phone number, 920-448-4470, in case the walk-in window changes.

Mailed documents travel through the P.O. box, so allow extra days. For a same-day closing, hand delivery before the earlier cutoff is the safer route.

Recording step by step for a seller

The title company normally does all of this. If you are filing on your own, here is the order that avoids a second trip.

  1. Copy the parcel number from the tax bill onto the deed.
  2. Compare the deed with the rejection list, especially the empty corner and return address.
  3. Prepare the transfer return showing the price or the exemption.
  4. Add a Swift Agreement to any paper package and name who gets the recorded copy.
  5. Arrive before the walk-in cutoff with the $30 recording fee and the transfer fee.
  6. Grab the emailed copy inside its seven-day window.

A cash buyer still needs a recorded deed and still triggers the transfer fee. The difference is that no lender is involved, so the paper stack is smaller and the closing date turns on when the deed is ready.

Brown County at a glance

Population here is 275,803, up 2.6 percent since 2020, spread over 118,788 housing units in the Green Bay metro area. Roughly 66.0 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $266,000. Median gross rent is $1,031. The two cities are Green Bay and De Pere, ringed by villages such as Allouez, Ashwaubenon, Bellevue, Howard, Suamico and Pulaski.

Property tax is a different office. The county treasurer takes first-installment payments for only some municipalities here, so read your bill to see who gets the check.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Brown County Register of Deeds hours?

Mornings and afternoons Monday to Thursday, with a shorter Friday. Hand-delivered real estate filings have an earlier cutoff than the general public hours, so call 920-448-4470 before a closing day.

Do I need a Swift Agreement to record a deed in Brown County?

Yes, for paper filings. Brown County records without a tag, so a completed Swift Agreement goes with the paper package. You then receive an emailed link good for three printed copies over seven days.

How do I search Brown County land records?

Use the Laredo system, which is by appointment only, and call 920-448-4470 to book. Many sellers skip this because the title company does the search for the sale.

How much is the real estate transfer fee in Brown County?

Statewide it is 30 cents per $100 of value, and the seller pays it under s. 77.22. Transfers by will, parent-to-child gifts and foreclosure deeds to the lender are among the exemptions.

Can the Brown County register record a deed that has a Social Security number?

No. Wisconsin law (s. 59.43(1m)) forbids recording any document that includes an individual's Social Security number, so redact it before you submit the deed.

What the office does

The Winnebago County Register of Deeds is where Oshkosh-area property records live, along with vital records and military discharges. The land side of the office files deeds, land contracts, mortgages, UCC realty filings, plats, certified survey maps and federal tax liens.

When a house in the county sells, the seller's deed to the buyer is filed here, and staff take the state transfer fee at that same visit. The phone number is 920-232-3390.

Recording and copy fees

Filing a deed costs $30 flat, and page count does not change it. The county's fee schedule traces that to Wisconsin Act 314 of 2010, and Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag) sets the identical $30 for any recordable document.

ServiceWinnebago County charge
Filing a deed, mortgage, land contract or satisfaction$30, flat
Plain copy of a filed document$2 for page one, then $1 per added page
Certification of a copy$1 extra
Subdivision, cemetery or condominium plat$50
State transfer fee$3 per $1,000 of value, rounded up to the next hundred, unless exempt

The office takes cash, money orders and personal checks. A card works only for orders placed in the office, and amounts up to $50 draw a $2.50 surcharge. Whoever asks for a service pays in advance, so have payment ready before the deed goes in.

The transfer fee

Thirty cents per $100 of value is the transfer fee, and the seller owes it. Staff collect it as the deed is handed in. The grantor, meaning the seller, bears the fee under state law, and any piece of $100 is charged as a whole $100.

The whole price counts. Wis. Stat. 77.21(3) measures a sale by every dollar paid or promised, including the balance of any lien on the property. For a gift, or a deed with token consideration, value means the likely open-market price. For a land contract, it means the total principal the buyer agrees to pay.

Of each fee collected, the county retains 20 percent by statute and sends the remainder to the state. The register is not obliged to test the reported value or an exemption claim, which leaves the buyer and seller answerable for their own figures.

Exempt transfers

A transfer escapes the fee only if it fits a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25, and the deed must give the reason by subsection number. These matter most to families and to sellers under pressure:

  • Gifts or near-gifts within a family: parent to child, stepparent to stepchild, parent to a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, or grandparent to grandchild.
  • A transfer between a person and a domestic partner.
  • Property that passes by will, by descent or by survivorship.
  • Foreclosure and deed-in-lieu transfers to a mortgage holder or a land contract seller.
  • A sale made for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A conveyance of real estate valued at $1,000 or less.

Exemptions are read narrowly. Court decisions summarized alongside the statute show that a move between two entities can be taxed even when family members own both. If a deed involves an LLC or a trust, check the exemption wording or ask the Register of Deeds before signing.

Filing the transfer return

You file a Real Estate Transfer Return with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue, then bring the receipt or exemption number along with the deed. Seller and buyer both sign. Without a finished return and the fee, the register has no authority to take the conveyance.

Filing now happens in My Tax Account, where nobody has to register or make a username and password. In that system you can submit, review or amend a return. The department's RETR page offers user guides, a walk-through video and a list of transfer fee exemptions. Send questions to retr@wisconsin.gov.

Every conveyance recorded here needs either an electronic transfer receipt plus the fee or an exemption number. Wis. Stat. 77.255 excuses a few exempt transfers from any return, so if you cannot tell which kind of deed you have, ask the register's office.

Deed format rules

Deeds that miss the state format may be turned away. Wis. Stat. 59.43(2m) sets the rules, among them:

  • A plain title for the document, set 0.5 inch to 6 inches below the top edge of page one.
  • An empty block of at least 3 inches by 3 inches in the upper right of page one, inside the margins, reserved for the recording stamp area.
  • Return-to information on page one, unless the document is recorded electronically.
  • The parcel identification number of every parcel involved, where the county requires it.
  • Pages 8.5 inches wide and 11 or 14 inches long, not hinged or joined along the top or sides.

The largest sheet allowed is 8.5 by 14 inches, one side of a sheet counts as a page, and an attached rider is a page of its own. Title companies and attorneys normally handle formatting in a sale. A seller drafting a quitclaim or family deed alone should check each item before mailing.

Tag-less and electronic recording

Since May 1, 2023, paper documents are recorded with no stamp, and the recorded version comes back to you by electronic means. Submit a signed SWIFT Agreement with your document to reach the official copy. You get a link that works for 7 days and prints up to 3 copies; after 3 copies or 7 days you pay regular copy fees.

Thirty days after recording, the paper original is shredded. To save it, include a self-addressed envelope with enough postage, or pick it up at the office within those 30 days, beginning the second business day after recording. It has no stamp and is not the official document. A list of companies that e-record real estate documents for Winnebago County is also available from the county.

Searching land records

Public terminals inside the office let you search, and paid online programs reach the same records. Records mostly reach back to 1850, and indexes to 1935. The office prefers appointments, offered in morning blocks (8:30 to 11:00 a.m.) and afternoon blocks (1:30 to 3:30 p.m.). Walk-ins are welcome on a first come basis, behind anyone who booked.

Tapestry serves occasional online users in real estate work. Laredo suits title firms and anyone who needs daily access. Both carry support and maintenance fees. Want to look at a recorded mortgage, an earlier deed or a lien before you list? Start at the terminals.

Check the county before you record

Oshkosh anchors the Oshkosh-Neenah metropolitan area, which is this county, home to 171,730 people in 2020. Oshkosh, Neenah, Omro, Menasha and Appleton are its cities, but Appleton lies mostly in Outagamie and Calumet counties and Menasha partly in Calumet County. An Appleton or Menasha mailing address can therefore sit in a different county than you assume.

Settle which county applies at the start, because the deed is recorded where the land lies.

What does recording a Winnebago County deed cost?

$30 for each document, whatever its length. Copies cost $2 for page one and $1 for every page after, with $1 more if you want it certified.

Who is responsible for the state transfer fee?

The seller does, in the role of grantor. At 30 cents per $100 of value, which the county words as $3 per $1,000 rounded up to the next hundred, the fee is collected as the deed is handed over.

Is a transfer return required before recording?

Nearly always. Recording requires a return signed by both parties, along with the fee or an exemption number. File it in My Tax Account, where no registration is needed.

Can I get an official copy of my deed after recording?

Yes. Submit a signed SWIFT Agreement with the document and the office sends a 7-day link for printing up to 3 copies. Later copies cost the standard fee.

How do I reach the Winnebago County Register of Deeds?

Phone 920-232-3390. Records on file include deeds, mortgages, land contracts, plats and vital records, and the public terminals are open by appointment or on a walk-in basis.

How the state transfer fee works

The grantor, meaning the seller, pays this charge: 30 cents on every $100 of value, with any leftover fraction counted as a full $100 (Wis. Stat. 77.22). Payment is collected as the deed comes in, and the amount is marked on the deed face. Of each dollar collected, twenty cents stays in the county and the rest is forwarded to the state.

The clerk won't audit your stated price. By statute the register need not work out true value or test an exemption claim, so accuracy rests with whoever signs the return.

Certain transfers owe nothing. Section 77.25 exempts, among others:

  • Family transfers for little or no payment, such as parent to child or grandparent to grandchild.
  • Land and buildings worth no more than $1,000.
  • A foreclosure deed or deed in lieu, when the grantee is the lender or land contract vendor.
  • Conveyances that come out of a delinquent tax or assessment sale.

An exempt deed must carry the matching subsection of 77.25 on its face.

Wis. Stat. 59.43(2m) lets the office bounce any instrument that departs from the standard layout. Here is what it looks for:

  • Reserve a square 3 inches on each side in the page one top right corner, because the stamp goes there.
  • Paper copies need return information on page one. E-filed ones don't.
  • The sheets should be white, at least 20 pound stock, 8.5 inches wide and either 11 or 14 inches long.
  • Ink must be black, blue or red, and sheets can't be hinged or joined on the top or sides.
  • Say who drafted the instrument.
  • Write or type the names of the grantor, the grantee and any notary so they can be read.

Keep Social Security numbers off the document entirely, because subsection (1m) bars recording one that shows it. A packet sent in as a single transaction can be returned whole if just one piece breaks the layout rules.

The office runs a free alert service worth joining. A notice reaches you each time something is filed under your name or on your parcel, so you can verify it. The county calls real estate fraud uncommon in Wisconsin, and enrollment is a single call to 920-683-4660.

Alerts pay off for absentee owners, vacant inherited houses and anyone mid-sale. Once your own deed is filed, the same alert watches for anything recorded later, and that is useful peace of mind after closing.

Order of steps on a sale

The deed and receipt then go to the counter or through an e-recording vendor, with the $30 fee and any transfer fee paid. Last, the register stamps the document and adds it to the permanent index. A buyer paying cash skips the lender's mortgage, so there is one less document to record, but the deed and return are still needed. Ask for a copy of the filed deed afterward, since certified copies cost only $1 extra.

Yes. File the Wisconsin Electronic Real Estate Transfer Return and print the receipt, which goes with the original deed. Only conveyances exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25(1) or (10m) skip it.

Typically no. Transfers by will, descent or survivorship are exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25(11). If the heir then sells to a buyer, that second conveyance carries the fee based on the price.

Local governments may not add a fee to a conveyance the state exempts (s. 77.256), and s. 77.255 says when an exempt transfer needs no return.

Deed format rules

Documents that stray from the layout in s. 59.43(2m) can be refused. Place the title anywhere from half an inch to six inches down page one. Keep an empty 3 inch by 3 inch box in the page's top right corner, within the margins, for recording information; without it the deed may not be recorded.

Old forms and online templates often miss these points, which is why such deeds come back. Have your title company or attorney read the final deed before signing.

Property taxes and your sale

Most real estate tax goes to the County Treasurer at 1516 Church Street, Stevens Point, (715) 346-1348, open weekdays 7:30 am to 4:30 pm. Installments are due January 31 and July 31, and the treasurer covers 23 of 28 municipalities for the first and 27 of 28 for the second. Stevens Point runs its own three installments, so city sellers pay the city. Almond, Belmont and Lanark (towns) and Milladore (village) keep their first installment local. Request an exact payoff from the right treasurer before closing.

  • Paying by check or cash, at the window or by mail, is free.
  • Vendor fees apply otherwise: 2.39 percent on credit cards, $3.95 for online debit, $1.50 per electronic check.

If taxes go unpaid

Miss an installment and you lose the right to pay in installments; interest of 1.5 percent a month then builds on what's unpaid. The sixth business day after the due date is when delinquency starts, since s. 74.11(7) and (8) give five working days of grace.

A balance open on September 1 leads the county to issue a tax certificate and mail notice of it. Two years remain to pay that year's tax before tax deed foreclosure starts. Auctions are listed on the county's Tax Deed Land Sale page.

Behind on taxes? The county names the Foundation for Rural Housing as a possible source of funds for delinquent taxes: 608-238-3448 or 888-400-5974.

Credits on the bill

Look for three credits on the bill. Every bill gets the school levy tax credit, and parcels with an improvement get the first dollar credit, both without any action from you. The lottery and gaming credit is different: it covers a primary residence, requires a claim, and applies to one parcel only. The Treasurer's page posts ratios, credits and mill rates for 2021 through 2025.

Searching parcels and recorded documents

Land records live at landinfo.co.portage.wi.gov, the same site the Treasurer uses for tax lookups and online payments. Type the parcel number by itself in the bill's format, because added terms shrink results. You can also try a property address or a first and last name.

Steps for a cash sale

Recording works the same for a cash buyer. The closing agent drafts the deed, files the eRETR naming both parties and forwards receipt, deed and fees. The buyer has no mortgage to record, though a satisfaction for any loan you're paying off still is. Ask which exemption, if any, fits, and confirm unpaid taxes come out of your proceeds.

Portage County in brief

The 2020 count was 70,377 people, and the 2025 estimate is 71,943. About 68.4 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied. Twenty-eight municipalities, from the City of Stevens Point to small towns like Alban, Hull and New Hope, all file deeds at this one office, but each decides who collects its first tax installment.

Frequently asked questions

Where does the deed go?

To the Register of Deeds/Land Description office. Submit the signed deed, eRETR receipt and fees as one packet, and call ahead about hours and payment types.

How big is the transfer fee?

It's 30 cents per $100 of value (Wis. Stat. 77.22(1)), the seller's cost, in addition to $30 for recording.

Is the eRETR required?

Yes, unless the transfer is exempt. Finish it on the state's revenue site, print the receipt, and give it to the register along with the deed.

Is an inherited house charged?

Not for the inheritance itself, which s. 77.25(11) exempts. A later sale by the heir is a fresh conveyance and does owe the fee.

When are taxes due?

First installment January 31, second July 31. The city of Stevens Point and a few towns and a village collect locally, so read your bill's coupons.

Where do you record a deed in Barron County, WI?

Barron County deeds are recorded by the county Register of Deeds, the office that holds both real estate records and vital records for the county. You will find it listed among the departments on the county website.

The office describes its purpose as guarding the official repository of property records and keeping that repository open to the public. Sellers should note one limit: nobody at the counter will run a real estate search for you. The title company or closing agent handles that order. You bring the finished deed to the register for recording.

Under s. 59.43 the register records each document presented that the law permits, marks it with the date, hour and minute, and works through documents in the order received.

Recording fees

A flat $30 covers recording for most documents in Barron County, set by s. 59.43(2)(ag). Whoever requests the service pays up front.

The rest of the state schedule is brief:

  • A deed, mortgage, satisfaction or similar recordable document: $30.
  • A cemetery, subdivision or condominium plat: $50.
  • Copies: $2 for page one, then $1 for every added page, and $1 more for a certification.

Getting your recorded paperwork back takes a little planning. A self-addressed stamped envelope brings a paper copy, and an email address brings a PDF. Without one of the two, the document is not returned, so tuck one into the packet. The Wisconsin Register of Deeds Association posts a recording and filing fee schedule as well.

How much is the Wisconsin transfer fee on a Barron County sale?

The charge is 30 cents per $100 of value on a taxable deed, or $3 per $1,000, and the seller owes it (s. 77.22). Barron County's median owner-occupied home value is $216,600, which gives a sense of the scale for a typical house.

Value means the whole price paid or to be paid, including liens. For a land contract, use the full principal the buyer agrees to pay. Payment goes to the register along with the deed, and both seller and buyer sign the return. Nobody at the register double-checks your stated value or exemption claim, so accuracy is on the signers. Of the fee, the county retains 20 percent and the state receives the balance (s. 77.24).

The return itself is now filed with the Department of Revenue through My Tax Account. Before you log in, collect the completed deed, each party's name, address, phone and email, a Social Security number, ITIN or FEIN for every seller and buyer, and the parcel numbers off the property tax bill.

Once the return is submitted, print the receipt and carry it to the register with the notarized deed and your payment. A few counties accept the packet electronically, so ask the Barron County office which route it prefers. If the property spans two counties, file a return for each. A value understated by 25 percent or more, or a wrongly claimed exemption, brings a penalty of $25 or 25 percent of the added fee, whichever is greater. For questions, email RETR@wisconsin.gov or phone 608-264-6885.

Transfers that owe no fee

  • gifts or nominal-price deals between parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, or grandparent and grandchild;

Wisconsin reads exemptions narrowly, and if the return does not offer the one you expected, the transfer owes the fee. A house moving within a family deserves a check of this list before anyone pays a fee that may not be owed.

Deed format rules for Barron County

A cash sale and recording

Where to record a deed

Doors are open from 7:45 am until 4:30 pm on weekdays, holidays excepted. Recording of real estate documents stops at 3:30 pm. Anything handed in after that is dated the next business day, so a seller who needs the same-day date should drop off the paperwork earlier.

Three delivery routes exist: e-recording, mail and a trip to the counter. Title companies, banks and law firms mostly use e-recording through vendors the county works with: Simplifile, CSC eRecording Solutions, Indecomm Global Services, eRecording Partners Network and hopdox. If you are selling without a title company, mail the deed or bring it yourself. The office sends the original back to whatever return address is printed on the deed.

What a deed must include

A deed that misses a formatting rule can come back to you, and that can delay the closing. Wis. Stat. 59.43(2m) is the source of the rules behind most rejections.

  • Leave the upper right corner of page one empty, a square measuring 3 inches by 3 inches, for the stamp.
  • On the first page, keep margins of half an inch at the top and a quarter inch at the sides and bottom.
  • Use 20 pound white letter or legal paper. Hinged pages are out.
  • Show who the document should be returned to and who drafted it.
  • Sign in original ink, with either an attorney's authentication or a notary's certificate of acknowledgment that shows a current commission date.
  • Keep Social Security numbers off the document. Section 59.43(1m)(a) bars the register from recording one that contains such a number.
  • Make every page clear enough to copy.

These are the common trouble spots, not a complete list. If the instrument is unusual, such as a correction deed or a plat, call (920) 929-3018 first.

Recording costs

The standard charge is $30 per real estate document, no matter how many pages it has. Plats cost $50. The statutes behind those amounts are 59.43(2)(ag) and 59.43(2)(h), and under 59.43(2g)(a) whoever requests the service pays up front.

Transfer fee basics

Thirty cents for every $100 of value, with any fraction rounded up, is the rate. That is $3 per $1,000. The grantor owes it under Wis. Stat. 77.22(1), which means the seller. Value in a sale is the whole price paid or still to be paid, counting the amount of any lien on the land. For a gift or a deed with token consideration, use the estimated open-market price (77.21(3)). For a land contract, use the total principal the buyer promises to pay.

The register takes the fee along with the deed and records the amount on it. When nothing is owed, the deed must say why by citing the matching part of 77.25. Staff are under no duty to test the value or an exemption claim, so filers carry that burden. Twenty percent of the fees stays in the county and the remainder moves to the state (77.24).

Transfers that owe no fee

The exemptions are in section 77.25 and are read strictly. These are the ones that matter to local families who sell, inherit or restructure ownership:

  • Passing property by will, descent or survivorship (77.25(11)).
  • Moving it within the family, from parent to child, stepparent to stepchild or grandparent to grandchild, for little or nothing (77.25(8)), or between a person and a domestic partner (77.25(8n)).
  • Handing it to a mortgage holder through foreclosure or by deed in lieu (77.25(14)).
  • Recording a deed that only confirms, corrects or reforms an earlier recorded conveyance, for nominal or no consideration (77.25(3)).
  • Trust transfers: trustee to beneficiary without real consideration (77.25(9)), or into a trust where a transfer to its beneficiary would be exempt (77.25(16)).
  • Real estate valued at $1,000 or less (77.25(13)).

A normal arm's-length house sale does not belong on this list. If you believe your deal does, have the closing attorney or title company name the exact subsection on the deed.

The electronic transfer return

Any conveyance of an ownership interest in real estate needs a return filed electronically with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue. Fill it out online, print the receipt, then send the receipt and any fee to the Register of Deeds with your deed. The deed will not be accepted otherwise. Under 77.22(1) both grantor and grantee sign, and 77.22(2) lets the Department of Revenue prescribe the form.

The department has been shifting the return into its My Tax Account system, so reach the filing screen through the link on the county page. Take return questions to RETR@wisconsin.gov. If you want to know whether a recorded deed has arrived, call the county office.

Searching and monitoring records

With the county's LandShark system you can search for, and buy copies of, recorded deeds, mortgages and easements dating to 1839. The office also has public terminals. Before June 1, 1994, the tract index book images apply, and grantor and grantee name index book images cover 1835 through 1985.

The free Land Notification service sends an email or text when a document is recorded under your name, your business name or a parcel identification number. Its purpose is to catch property fraud early, which is useful for vacant lots, inherited houses and rentals that rarely get a visit. To set up alerts, call (920) 929-3018.

Local facts and taxes at closing

The county seat is the city of Fond du Lac, at the southern end of Lake Winnebago. Population is 104,669 across 46,496 housing units. Owners occupy about 70.7 percent of them, the median home value is $222,800 and median gross rent is $960.

Property tax comes up at closing too. For a deed recorded during the year, Wis. Stat. 74.15 divides that year's taxes if the contract is silent. The grantor reimburses the grantee one-twelfth of last year's assessed taxes for each elapsed month, counting the sale month when the deed is recorded after the 15th. Purchase contracts usually swap this for their own proration wording, so read yours and ask the title company for the final amount.

Selling for cash leaves the recording steps unchanged: right format, return receipt, both fees. Only the lender's paperwork goes away.

Frequently asked questions

What time does the Fond du Lac County Register of Deeds close?

The office stays open to 4:30 pm on weekdays, yet real estate documents are recorded only from 7:45 am to 3:30 pm. A deed that arrives later gets the next business day.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Fond du Lac County?

A standard real estate document is $30 regardless of length, and a plat is $50. A copy is $2.00 for page one and $1.00 per added page, with $1.00 more for certification.

Who pays the Wisconsin real estate transfer fee?

The grantor, who is the seller. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) sets 30 cents per $100 of value, which is $3 per $1,000, unless an exemption under 77.25 applies.

Do I need a title company to record a deed in Fond du Lac County?

No. Deeds can be e-recorded, mailed or delivered by hand, and you can prepare the forms yourself or use an attorney. The deed must still meet the format rules and come with the return receipt and fees.

Can I be alerted if someone records a document against my property?

Yes, through the free Land Notification service. It emails or texts you when a document is recorded under your name or a parcel number you enter. Sign up from the Register of Deeds page.

Office address, hours and phone

Marinette County's Register of Deeds is at 1926 Hall Ave, Marinette, WI 54143, open Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. Phone 715-732-7551 or fax 715-732-7556. FedEx and UPS packages go to a different address: 1925 Ella Court, Marinette, WI 54143.

This is the county's official repository for real estate instruments and vital records, and it collects the fees Wisconsin statutes require. On a house sale, the deed, any mortgage payoff paperwork and the transfer return all pass through the counter.

The Marinette County housing market in brief

Marinette County had 41,872 residents in 2020 and an estimated 42,574 in July 2025, up 1.7 percent. About 28.3 percent of residents are 65 or older. The 2020 census counted 29,189 housing units with a vacancy figure of 35.8 percent. Among occupied homes, 81.6 percent are owner-occupied. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $158,600, median gross rent is $795 a month, and 215 building permits were issued in 2025.

Marinette is the county seat, and every deed in the county, rural or not, is filed at the Hall Ave office.

Fees for recording a deed

Wisconsin's statutory fee schedule applies at this office. Recording a document is $30, and the person requesting a service pays in advance under Wis. Stat. 59.43(2g). A copy is $2 for the first page and $1 for each added page, and certifying it costs $1 more. The county's User Fees page, under the Register of Deeds menu, shows the full list, and staff can explain any other charge.

What the office does with your deed

State law (Wis. Stat. 59.43(1c)) gives the register these tasks for each filing:

  • Take documents in the order they arrive.
  • Stamp the date, hour and minute of recording, which serves as prima facie evidence of when it was recorded.
  • Assign a unique number that continues the series.
  • Preserve originals, images and indexes permanently, with nothing discarded.
  • Write the transfer fee paid on a conveyance, or the reason it's exempt.
  • Send the recorded document to whoever you name, once you supply postage.

When a deed and a mortgage reach the same property close together, the stamp shows which came first. Facing a closing date? Send the deed early.

How the transfer fee works

On a non-exempt conveyance the seller owes 30 cents for each $100 of value, with partial hundreds rounded up. For a land contract, value means the total principal the buyer agrees to pay. For a gift or exchange, it is the estimated open market price.

Buyer and seller both sign a transfer return. The state has required electronic filing since July 1, 2009, unless the Department of Revenue grants a hardship waiver. The county's site has Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Returns under the Register of Deeds menu. Each month by the 15th, the register sends returns and money to the county treasurer, and 20 percent remains with the county. Local governments can't tack their own charge onto a conveyance the state fee exempts.

Transfers that owe no state fee

Wis. Stat. 77.25 names the exempt conveyances. Several matter to private owners:

  • Transfers by will, descent or survivorship.
  • A trustee's deed to a beneficiary, or a deed between agent and principal, with no real payment.
  • Parent to child or grandparent to grandchild, for nominal or no consideration.
  • A conveyance made only to give or release security for a debt.
  • A deed on foreclosure, or in place of it, to the lender or land contract seller.
  • A deed that completes a land contract after the proper fee was paid on the contract.

Exemptions are read narrowly. A transfer that sits near one of these without fitting squarely may still owe the fee, so check with a Wisconsin attorney if yours is unclear.

E-recording and online records

You can do both. Two e-recording services are listed: CSC (Corporation Services Corp) at 866-403-5272 and Simplifile at 800-460-5657. For searching, LandShark covers documents recorded at this office from 1990 forward. Registering and viewing the index costs nothing. One account type is built for daily users such as title firms that view and buy images, and another suits occasional users.

Someone without a real estate background may do better to visit the office for help finding a document. For anything older than 1990, call 715-732-7551 to learn how to get a copy.

Land contracts and gifts

Not every transfer is a plain sale, and the fee base shifts with the type. A land contract is valued at the total principal the buyer agrees to pay. A gift or an exchange is valued at the estimated open market price. When the land contract is later paid off and a deed completes it, no second fee is due if the proper fee was already paid on the contract. Say so on the deed and cite the exemption. If you are unsure which value or exemption fits, a Wisconsin attorney can sort it out before you reach the counter, since staff won't make that call for you.

Getting copies after closing

After recording, the register sends the document to the person you named, provided you supplied enough postage. Keep that copy with your closing file. If you need another one later, request a copy at $2 for the first page and $1 for each page after, and add $1 if it must be certified. Certified copies are what lenders and courts usually ask for. For records from 1990 forward, LandShark can show you the index before you order, which saves a trip.

Steps for a seller

Doing the paperwork yourself? Go in this order, so nothing bounces back to you. Sign a deed that names its drafter. Both parties then complete the electronic transfer return, and you print the receipt. Take or mail the deed and receipt with the $30 fee, plus the transfer fee unless an exemption applies and is cited. The register stamps the time, numbers the document and files it permanently. Most sellers let the title company or closing attorney do all this. A buyer paying cash changes little here, because the deed and return are required either way. Call the office before you send anything unusual, like a land contract deed, and ask whether a cover note would help staff route it. Keep the receipt and your recorded copy together in one folder for whoever handles the next sale.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Marinette County Register of Deeds open?

Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. The office is at 1926 Hall Ave, Marinette, WI 54143, phone 715-732-7551. FedEx and UPS deliveries go to 1925 Ella Court.

What does recording a deed cost in Marinette County?

Recording is $30, paid in advance. Unless the transfer is exempt, the state transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value is added. A copy is $2 for page one and $1 for each added page.

Can a deed be e-recorded in Marinette County?

Yes, through CSC (866-403-5272) or Simplifile (800-460-5657). Your closing agent can tell you whether they'll file this way.

Who pays the transfer fee on a Marinette County sale?

The seller, called the grantor in the statute. The register collects it when the deed comes in, and buyer and seller both sign the electronic transfer return.

Can I search Marinette County records online?

Yes. LandShark has documents recorded from 1990 forward, and registering and viewing the index is free. Daily users who buy images have their own plan, and older records can be requested at 715-732-7551.

Location, hours and cutoffs

Vilas County's deed office is inside the courthouse, 330 Court Street, Eagle River. The phone is 715.479.3660. Weekday hours run 8am to 4pm, and holidays are closed days.

Paper has to be in hand by 3:00pm. Electronic filings face an earlier line, 2:45pm. Payment at the window is cash or check only, so settle that before you make the drive. Staff cannot write a deed or explain the law to you. Use a title company, a closing agent or a lawyer for that.

What the office records in a sale

Filings here include deeds, land contracts, mortgages and real property financing statements. Records of births, deaths and marriages sit in the same office. The register follows Wis. Stat. 59.43(1c): each item is stamped to the minute, numbered in sequence and added to the public index.

The stamp settles who came first. Under Wis. Stat. 706.08(1)(a), a later purchaser who paid value honestly and recorded first beats an earlier buyer whose deed was never filed. Do not let a signed deed sit unrecorded.

Forms the county posts that families and sellers often need:

  • Standard Form and Document Requirements, the layout rules a filing must meet
  • Termination of Decedent's Property Interest, with its own instruction sheet
  • Designation of TOD Beneficiary
  • Registration of Firm Name, also with instructions

Recording and copy fees

A deed costs $30 to record, set by Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). Separately, a seller pays the transfer fee to the state, which is 30 cents per $100 of value. If you order copies, page one is $2, later pages $1 each, and a certificate adds $1.

Payment of the transfer fee happens when the deed is handed in. Wis. Stat. 77.24 lets the county retain 20 percent, with the balance going to the state.

The transfer return (RETR)

No deed goes in alone. Attached to it is the RETR, an online return the Wisconsin Department of Revenue hosts in My Tax Account, signed by buyer and seller alike. If the return is incomplete and no exemption applies, the register cannot take the conveyance.

Before you open the form, collect the finished deed, contact details (address, phone, email) for each party, their Social Security, ITIN or FEIN numbers, and the parcel numbers off the property tax bill. The Department of Revenue overview walks through the list.

Submit, print the receipt, and walk it into the Register of Deeds with the notarized deed and your check. Because the state recently changed the RETR system, look at the state site for the current screens. Reporting a value that is 25 percent or more too low, or claiming an exemption that does not fit, brings a penalty of $25 or 25 percent of the extra fee, whichever is larger.

Exempt transfers

Plenty of family and estate transfers escape the fee, though a return may still be needed. Wis. Stat. 77.25 and the state's exemption guide name these among others: inheritance by will, descent or survivorship; spouse to spouse; parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, or grandparent and grandchild when little or nothing is paid; a foreclosure deed, or deed in lieu, handed to a mortgage holder or land contract seller; transfers on death under Wis. Stat. 705.15 along with a TOD beneficiary designation; and property worth $1,000 or less.

The deed itself must cite the exemption by subsection number. If yours is missing from the dropdown for your document and parties, treat the transfer as taxable. Nobody at the counter checks value or exemptions, so the signers carry that responsibility.

Can I record a Vilas County deed electronically?

Yes. Three companies transmit e-recordings to this office: Simplifile at 800-460-5657, CSC eRecording Solutions at 866-652-0111 and Hopdox at 385-501-5103. Your title company or closing agent typically does the upload. Beat the 2:45pm cutoff.

A paper deed must meet Wis. Stat. 59.43(2m) or risk refusal. Have your preparer check the layout. The first page needs an empty 3 inch by 3 inch square in the top right corner. Sheets should be 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, printed in black, blue or red ink with margins of at least a quarter inch. The deed also has to show a parcel identification number, plain grantor and grantee names and the drafter's name.

The Register of Deeds page also offers Land Notification Alerts, including text alerts, so you hear when something is recorded against your property.

Lakefront, forest land and unpaid taxes

Vilas County counted 23,047 residents and 24,486 housing units in 2020. A full 55.9 percent of the units were vacant, the mark of a cabin and second-home market. Among occupied homes, 81.1 percent were owner-occupied.

Water and woods both show up on the return. It asks for feet of water frontage and for acres in Managed Forest Law or Private Forest Crop programs, and the Department of Natural Resources must hear about ownership changes on enrolled land.

Request a current statement from the county treasurer before closing. Any unpaid tax can then be paid at the table.

Seller checklist for recording day

Line everything up a day ahead. A title company, closing agent or attorney drafts the deed. You sign it before a notary. The transfer return is finished, the receipt printed and any exemption number jotted down. Then either bring cash or a check to the window or let the closing agent e-record before 2:45pm. A paper deed sent by mail needs time to arrive before 3:00pm.

A cash sale follows these same steps. With no lender in the picture, the closing date can be built around the recording cutoffs rather than a loan deadline.

Once recorded, ask for a copy for your closing file. A certified copy adds a dollar, and it is the version an agency or lender tends to want later.

If you are an heir rather than a seller, the same office can help you sort out which form applies. Ask whether a Termination of Decedent's Property Interest or a TOD beneficiary designation fits your situation, and read the instruction sheet before you fill it in. Because staff cannot give legal advice, bring questions about wording to an attorney, and bring questions about format, fees and cutoffs to the counter. A call to 715.479.3660 before you travel can save a wasted trip, especially when the deadline is near.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Vilas County?

$30 to record, per Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag). A seller adds the state transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, except where an exemption applies.

What are the Vilas County Register of Deeds hours?

Open weekdays 8am to 4pm, closed holidays. Paper filings are due by 3:00pm and e-recordings by 2:45pm. At the window, pay with cash or a check.

Who pays the Wisconsin transfer fee when a house sells?

The grantor, which means the seller. The statute (77.22(1)) puts the fee on that party, and the register collects it at submission.

Do I pay a transfer fee when I inherit a house in Vilas County?

Not when the house passes by will, descent or survivorship (Wis. Stat. 77.25(11)). The exemption number must still appear on the deed or return, and the county's forms include a Termination of Decedent's Property Interest.

What happens if a deed is never recorded?

A later buyer who pays value honestly and records first can win out over it (Wis. Stat. 706.08(1)(a)). File right away to protect the new owner.
